questions.question: You are building an internal Q&A assistant named Alex with the OpenAI-compatible SDK and Qwen-Max. You want every reply to stay in character as a helpful assistant for an educational content company, regardless of what employees ask. Where should this persona and task description be placed?

options.text: In a message with role "assistant" placed at the start of the messages list
options.explanation: The assistant role holds the model's own previous replies in the conversation history; it is not the slot for setting the model's role and task.

options.text: Prepended to every user question inside the "user" message content
options.explanation: This mixes instructions with the employee's question. The lesson keeps the user message for the user's input and sets the role and task separately.

options.text: In a message with role "system" at the start of the messages list
options.explanation: The lesson's code comments state that the system message is used to set the role and task of the LLM, which is exactly how the Alex persona is defined.

options.text: In the model parameter, for example model="qwen-max-alex"
options.explanation: The model parameter only selects which model to call (such as qwen-max); it does not carry persona instructions.

questions.takeaway: Use the system message to set the model's role and task; user messages carry the user's input.

questions.question: A developer is about to share a notebook that calls Model Studio. The current code contains the line api_key="sk-..." with the full key in plain text. What approach does the course recommend for handling the key?

options.text: Store the key in an environment variable and read it in code, for example with os.getenv("DASHSCOPE_API_KEY")
options.explanation: The course describes environment variables as the safer, more maintainable approach: the key is not exposed when code is shared, and rotation does not require editing plaintext references.

options.text: Keep the key in the source code but split it into several string fragments that are concatenated at runtime
options.explanation: The key is still present in the shared source and must still be edited manually on rotation, so the core risk remains.

options.text: Keep the key hardcoded but add a comment asking readers not to copy it
options.explanation: A comment does not prevent exposure; hardcoding is exactly what the course identifies as a security risk.

options.text: Print the full key at startup so the developer can confirm it was loaded correctly
options.explanation: The course's setup only displays the first five characters followed by asterisks, specifically so the configuration can be verified without exposing the full key.

questions.takeaway: Never hardcode API keys; load them from environment variables and mask them when displaying.

questions.question: An employee asks the bot "What project management tools does our company use?" and then follows up with "How do I apply for an account for this tool?" The bot answers the follow-up as if it has no idea which tool is meant. Which changes to the calling code are needed so the follow-up is understood?

options.text: After each call, append the model's reply to the history as a message with role "assistant"
options.explanation: The lesson appends each reply as an assistant message so it can be used in the next round; without it, the model never sees what tool it previously named.

options.text: Set temperature=0 so the model consistently remembers earlier turns
options.explanation: Temperature only reshapes the next-token probability distribution; it has no effect on whether earlier turns are available to the model.

options.text: Pass the complete conversation history list as the messages parameter on every call
options.explanation: The LLM generates responses based on all messages in the messages list, so the full history must be sent each time.

options.text: Send only the system message and the latest user question, relying on the server to keep track of earlier rounds
options.explanation: The lesson keeps context by resending the history in the messages list; sending only the latest question is exactly what causes the follow-up to lose its reference.

options.text: Append each new user question to the history list before making the call
options.explanation: The lesson adds the user question to conversation_history first and then calls the model with that list.

questions.takeaway: Multi-round conversation works by keeping system, user and assistant messages in one list and sending the whole list each call.

questions.question: Your multi-round FAQ bot works in testing and is now going to production, where some employees hold very long conversations and expect to resume them the next day. Which considerations from the course apply?

options.text: Once the history is sent in the first call, the model retains it between requests, so later calls only need the newest message
options.explanation: The course's approach resends the full history in the messages list on every call; nothing in the lesson suggests the model retains it between requests.

options.text: Conversation history occupies space in the context window, so long histories may need to be truncated or summarized
options.explanation: This is one of the lesson's explicit tips for multi-round conversations.

options.text: Enabling stream=True compresses the history so it takes up less of the context window
options.explanation: Streaming only changes how the output is delivered; it does not alter how much input the history consumes.

options.text: History usually needs to be persistently stored, for example in a database, to support conversations across sessions
options.explanation: The lesson notes that production environments typically persist history to support continuous conversations across sessions.

questions.takeaway: Conversation history costs context-window space and must be persisted by the application for cross-session continuity.

questions.question: Users complain that the Q&A bot shows a blank screen for about 20 seconds before the whole answer appears at once. You add stream=True to the API call. What effect should you expect?

options.text: The model generates a shorter answer so the total time drops below a few seconds
options.explanation: Streaming does not shorten the answer; the same content is produced, just delivered progressively.

options.text: Answer quality improves slightly because the model can revise earlier tokens while streaming
options.explanation: The course states that streaming leaves the model's reasoning and the quality of the final answer unchanged.

options.text: The model switches to greedy decoding, so answers become fully deterministic
options.explanation: Streaming is unrelated to the decoding strategy; randomness is governed by parameters like temperature and top_p.

options.text: Content is sent incrementally as it is generated, so users see partial results immediately while the final answer stays the same
options.explanation: This matches the course: streaming changes only how content is displayed, improving user experience without changing the answer's quality.

questions.takeaway: Streaming improves perceived latency by returning tokens as they are generated; it does not change the answer.

questions.question: You call client.chat.completions.create(model="qwen-max", messages=msgs, stream=True) and iterate over the returned object with for chunk in response. Which expression gives the newly generated text in each chunk, as used in the course?

options.text: chunk.choices[0].message.content
options.explanation: message.content is how the course reads the complete reply from a non-streaming response, not the incremental text in a stream chunk.

options.text: chunk.choices[0].delta.content
options.explanation: The course's streaming generator yields chunk.choices[0].delta.content for each chunk.

options.text: chunk.output.text
options.explanation: The course's OpenAI-compatible streaming code does not read an output.text field; it reads the delta of the first choice.

options.text: chunk.choices[0].usage
options.explanation: Usage is token accounting, not generated text; in the course's reasoning-model example it appears on a chunk whose choices list is empty.

questions.takeaway: In streaming mode, read each chunk's choices[0].delta.content; in non-streaming mode, read choices[0].message.content.

questions.question: During testing you ask Qwen-Max "What tools should our company use for project management?" twice. The two answers are worded differently, and both recommend generic tools such as Jira, Trello or Asana rather than the tools your company actually uses. Which explanations are consistent with the course?

options.text: Using stream=True is what makes the wording differ between the two calls
options.explanation: Streaming only changes how output is displayed; the variation comes from how the next token is chosen.

options.text: Many online services use stochastic sampling decoding by default, so identical inputs can yield slightly different answers
options.explanation: The course attributes varying answers to stochastic sampling methods such as top-p and top-k being used by default.

options.text: The model has broad general knowledge but no access to your company's specific context, such as its current toolchain
options.explanation: The course notes that the model lacks company-specific context like the toolchain, team size or budget, so it falls back on commonly used tools.

options.text: The model is retrained between the two calls, so its knowledge changes from one request to the next
options.explanation: Nothing in the course suggests retraining between calls; differences come from sampling, and generic advice from missing private context.

questions.takeaway: Answers vary because of stochastic sampling, and they are generic because the model lacks private company knowledge.

questions.question: The course explains how an LLM turns the partial input "ACP is a very" into a full sentence. Which sequence correctly orders the stages of that text generation process?

options.text: Token Embedding, Tokenization, Model Inference, Output Text, Decoding & Autoregression
options.explanation: Embedding needs token IDs, so tokenization must come first; output text is produced only after decoding.

options.text: Tokenization, Model Inference, Token Embedding, Decoding & Autoregression, Output Text
options.explanation: Inference runs on the embedding vectors, so embedding must happen before model inference, not after.

options.text: Tokenization, Token Embedding, Model Inference, Decoding & Autoregression, Output Text
options.explanation: This is the five-stage order given in the course.

options.text: Tokenization, Token Embedding, Decoding & Autoregression, Model Inference, Output Text
options.explanation: Decoding needs the logits produced by model inference, so inference must come before decoding.

questions.takeaway: Text generation goes: tokenization, embedding, model inference, decoding/autoregression, then output text.

questions.question: While watching a streamed answer, a colleague notices that words sometimes appear in pieces and spaces show up at odd moments. Which description of tokens explains this?

options.text: Each token is always one complete word, but the network delays some words more than others
options.explanation: The course states that tokens are not necessarily complete words, so the premise is wrong.

options.text: Tokens are usually sub-word or character fragments, each mapped to an integer ID, and spaces or punctuation can be encoded as tokens
options.explanation: This matches the course, which uses exactly this point to explain why streamed words can appear in chunks.

options.text: Tokens are fixed-length blocks of four characters, so word boundaries are ignored
options.explanation: The course describes tokens as sub-word or character fragments from a tokenizer vocabulary, not fixed-length blocks.

options.text: Each token ID encodes how important the word is, so higher IDs are sent first
options.explanation: The course points out that ID values are not inherently meaningful; ID 500 is not more important than ID 50.

questions.takeaway: Tokens are sub-word fragments with integer IDs, which is why streamed text can arrive mid-word.

questions.question: "Dog chases cat" and "cat chases dog" contain the same tokens but mean different things. According to the course, what in the token embedding stage allows the model to tell them apart?

options.text: The tokenizer assigns larger IDs to tokens that appear later in the sentence
options.explanation: Token IDs come from the vocabulary and carry no order information; the course stresses that ID values are not inherently meaningful.

options.text: The embedding matrix stores a separate row for each word in each possible position
options.explanation: The embedding matrix is looked up by token ID only; order is supplied by a separate mechanism.

options.text: The temperature parameter weights earlier tokens more heavily than later ones
options.explanation: Temperature reshapes the output probability distribution during decoding; it has nothing to do with word order in the input.

options.text: Positional encoding is added to each token vector, because the standard transformer has no built-in sense of word order
options.explanation: The course explains that positional encoding must be added so the model can distinguish which word comes first, third, and so on.

questions.takeaway: Embeddings capture meaning; positional encoding supplies word order the transformer otherwise lacks.

questions.question: During autoregressive generation, each newly chosen token is appended to the input and the model predicts again. Which conditions end this loop?

options.text: A special End-of-Sequence (EOS) token is generated
options.explanation: The course lists generation of an EOS token, such as <|im_end|> for Qwen3, as a stopping condition.

options.text: The probability of the most likely candidate token falls below 50%
options.explanation: Low top-token probability just means a flatter distribution; the course does not list it as a reason to stop.

options.text: The cumulative probability of the candidate set reaches the top_p threshold
options.explanation: Reaching the top_p threshold defines the sampling candidate set for one token; it does not end generation.

options.text: The pre-set maximum generation length is reached
options.explanation: The course lists hitting the maximum generation length as a stopping condition.

options.text: A user-specified stop word sequence is generated
options.explanation: The course lists generation of a user-specified stop sequence as a stopping condition.

questions.takeaway: Generation stops on an EOS token, the maximum length, or a user-defined stop sequence.

questions.question: Your team uses Qwen-Max to generate code snippets, and reviewers complain that results vary noticeably between runs for the same request. Following the course's recommendations, which adjustment is most appropriate?

options.text: Lower the temperature, so the probability distribution concentrates on a few high-probability tokens
options.explanation: The course recommends a lower temperature for clear answers such as code generation, because it sharpens the distribution and makes output more deterministic.

options.text: Raise the temperature toward 1.9, so the model has more options to find the correct code
options.explanation: A higher temperature flattens the distribution and increases diversity, which makes run-to-run variation worse.

options.text: Enable stream=True, so tokens are fixed as soon as they are produced
options.explanation: Streaming only changes how content is displayed; it does not reduce sampling randomness.

options.text: Raise top_p to its maximum, so the model always considers every candidate token
options.explanation: A higher top_p broadens the candidate set and increases diversity; the course recommends lower top_p for code generation.

questions.takeaway: For tasks needing clear, stable answers like code, lower the temperature (or top_p).

questions.question: For the next token after "ACP is a very", the model's candidates are: informative 50%, fun 25%, enlightening 20%, boring 5%. With top_p=0.7, which tokens form the candidate set from which the next token is sampled?

options.text: informative only
options.explanation: informative alone reaches only 0.5, which is below 0.7. The set must be the smallest one whose cumulative probability is at least the threshold, so more tokens are needed.

options.text: informative and fun
options.explanation: Sorted by probability, the cumulative total is 0.5, then 0.75. Adding fun is the first point that reaches at least 0.7, so these two tokens form the set.

options.text: informative, fun and enlightening
options.explanation: The set would total 0.95, but top_p takes the smallest set that reaches the threshold, and 0.7 is already reached after fun.

options.text: All four tokens, with probabilities rescaled to 70% of their original values
options.explanation: top_p does not scale probabilities; it filters the sorted candidates down to the smallest set whose cumulative probability meets the threshold.

questions.takeaway: top_p keeps the smallest set of top-ranked tokens whose cumulative probability is at least the threshold.

sources.heading: 2.2.2 top_p: Control the sampling range of the candidate token set

questions.question: A compliance team requires the FAQ bot to give the same answer whenever the same question is asked. You experiment with temperature, top_p and seed. Which statements about these settings are accurate according to the course?

options.text: Setting temperature=0 together with a fixed seed guarantees identical output on every call
options.explanation: The course says that even with temperature 0, a very low top_p and the same seed, results may still differ because of factors like distributed systems or output optimization.

options.text: temperature=0 minimizes randomness but does not guarantee identical outputs every time
options.explanation: The course explicitly notes that temperature 0 minimizes randomness without guaranteeing identical outputs.

options.text: With the same seed, prompt and generation parameters, the model will typically produce identical outputs, though full determinism is not guaranteed
options.explanation: This matches the course's description of the seed parameter, including the caveat about hardware-level non-determinism.

options.text: An extremely low top_p such as 0.0001 theoretically selects only the highest-probability token, but slight randomness may remain in practice
options.explanation: The course says this setting makes output very stable, yet distributed systems and output adjustments can still introduce slight randomness.

questions.takeaway: temperature, top_p and seed can greatly reduce randomness, but none of them guarantees bit-identical output.

questions.question: According to the parameter ranges given in the course for Qwen-Max, which configuration is valid?

options.text: temperature=2.0, top_p=0.8
options.explanation: Qwen-Max's temperature range is [0, 2), so 2.0 itself is excluded.

options.text: temperature=0.7, top_p=0
options.explanation: Qwen-Max's top_p range is (0, 1], so 0 is excluded.

options.text: temperature=0.7, top_p=1.5
options.explanation: top_p is a cumulative-probability threshold with a range of (0, 1], so 1.5 is out of range.

options.text: temperature=1.9, top_p=1.0
options.explanation: 1.9 is within [0, 2) and 1.0 is within (0, 1], so both values are valid; the course itself runs an experiment with temperature=1.9.

questions.takeaway: For Qwen-Max, temperature is in [0, 2) with a default of 0.7, and top_p is in (0, 1] with a default of 0.8.

sources.heading: 2.2.2 top_p: Control the sampling range of the candidate token set

questions.question: Alex is building a writing assistant. Every time he asks for an article on "the development of artificial intelligence", the generated articles are very similar to each other. Which parameter changes would help produce more varied content?

options.text: Increase temperature, for example into the 0.7 to 0.9 range
options.explanation: The course attributes this lack of creativity to a temperature that is too low and suggests raising it to about 0.7 to 0.9.

options.text: Set top_p to 0.001
options.explanation: A very low top_p restricts sampling to almost only the top token, which makes output even more uniform.

options.text: Set top_k to 1
options.explanation: top_k=1 selects only the highest-probability token, which the course says produces stable output that lacks variation and creativity.

options.text: Fix the seed parameter to the same value on every request
options.explanation: A fixed seed with the same prompt and parameters is meant to make sampling reproducible, which works against variety.

options.text: Increase top_p, for example to 0.9
options.explanation: The course suggests top_p around 0.9 to expand the range of word selection, which increases diversity.

questions.takeaway: To increase variety, raise temperature and/or top_p; low top_p, top_k=1 or a fixed seed push toward sameness.

sources.heading: 2.2.2 top_p: Control the sampling range of the candidate token set

questions.question: Besides temperature and top_p, Qwen series models support a top_k parameter. What happens when top_k is set to 1?

options.text: The model samples uniformly from all tokens in the vocabulary
options.explanation: top_k restricts selection to the k most probable tokens, so k=1 is the most restrictive case, not the broadest.

options.text: The model returns only one token and then stops generating
options.explanation: top_k controls how each next token is chosen, not how many tokens are generated in total.

options.text: The model only selects the highest-probability token, making output stable but lacking variation
options.explanation: This matches the course's description of top_k=1.

options.text: The model picks the single best candidate path using beam search with one beam per sentence
options.explanation: The course describes top_k as a sampling method over the k most probable tokens, not a beam-search setting.

questions.takeaway: top_k limits sampling to the k most probable tokens; top_k=1 always picks the most probable token.

questions.question: A new engineer is tuning the FAQ bot for the first time and wants to understand how temperature and top_p each affect the output. What approach does the course advise?

options.text: Adjust one parameter at a time to understand its individual effect, then combine them for finer control once familiar
options.explanation: The course recommends that beginners change one parameter at a time, while noting that the two are commonly used together in practice.

options.text: Never use temperature and top_p together, because they cancel each other out
options.explanation: The course says the two parameters are commonly used together in practice; they influence randomness in different ways rather than cancelling out.

options.text: Always set both to their maximum values first, then lower them together until the output looks acceptable
options.explanation: Changing both at once makes it hard to see each parameter's individual effect, which is what the course advises beginners to avoid.

options.text: Leave both parameters at their defaults and adjust only the seed parameter
options.explanation: The seed is for reproducibility; it does not replace temperature and top_p as the controls for creativity and consistency.

questions.takeaway: When learning, change temperature or top_p one at a time; combine them later for fine control.

questions.question: To let the bot answer company-specific questions, a developer pastes the entire employee document library into the system prompt of every request. Which problems does the course associate with this approach?

options.text: The model's weights are updated with the document library, so its general knowledge gradually degrades
options.explanation: Putting knowledge in the prompt involves no model changes; updating weights is what fine-tuning or training does.

options.text: Long system prompts force temperature to 0, which removes all variation from answers
options.explanation: Prompt length has no effect on the temperature setting; the course does not describe any such interaction.

options.text: The input may exceed token limits, preventing the model from generating a response
options.explanation: The course warns that large background data can exceed token limits so that no response is generated.

options.text: Overly long inputs can reduce model efficiency
options.explanation: The course notes that introducing large amounts of background data can reduce model efficiency.

questions.takeaway: Putting knowledge in the prompt is cheap, but prompts have length limits; RAG retrieves only the relevant snippets instead.

sources.heading: ⚙️ 3. Enable LLMs to answer private knowledge questions

questions.question: You are designing a RAG pipeline for the company's internal documents. Which steps belong to the indexing phase rather than the retrieval and generation phase?

options.text: Searching the vector database for the snippets most relevant to the user's query
options.explanation: Searching based on the user's query happens in the retrieval and generation phase, after indexing is complete.

options.text: Splitting the knowledge documents into chunks
options.explanation: The course describes splitting content into chunks as part of the indexing phase.

options.text: Converting each chunk into an embedding using specialized models
options.explanation: The course places the conversion of chunks into embeddings in the indexing phase.

options.text: Combining the retrieved snippets with the original question and passing them to the LLM
options.explanation: Combining retrieved results with the question for the LLM is the generation part of the retrieval and generation phase.

options.text: Storing the embeddings in a vector database
options.explanation: The course says the indexing phase ends with embeddings stored in a vector database for fast similarity search.

questions.takeaway: Indexing = chunk, embed, store in a vector DB; retrieval and generation = search, combine with the query, generate.
